newsitem.title: USA: Oil companies battle higher Superfund taxes.
newsitem.headline: Oil companies battle higher Superfund taxes.

text.p: Oil companies said Wednesday they feared a Senate Republican proposal to reform the Superfund toxic waste cleanup programme could result in higher taxes on the oil industry.

The American Petroleum Institute urged lawmakers to revise the Superfund taxes on oil and chemicals and the corporate environmental tax to lighten the oil industry's share before they renew the taxes, which expired in 1995.
"Superfund sites are a broad societal problem, and taxes raised to remediate these sites should be broadly based rather than focused on specific industries," API said.

The three taxes, which the administration and Senate Republicans want to renew, used to put about $1.5 billion a year into the Superfund trust fund that the government uses to cover its toxic waste cleanup costs.

In testimony to the Senate Environment Committee, API said oil companies had historically paid more than half of the taxes for the trust fund, while they were responsible for less than 10 percent of the contamination at Superfund sites.
"This inequity is of paramount concern to API members and has caused the industry to focus on those elements that affect the costs of the programme," API said.

About three-quarters of cleanups of the nation's worst toxic waste dumps today are paid for by the companies that used the sites. The government covers cleanup costs where responsible parties cannot be found or are unable to pay.

The Senate Republican bill introduced this year would make the government pay more cleanup costs, making it pick up the costs for all parties who dumped waste in private landfills, and pick up some costs for cleaning up municipal landfills.
API said before it could support the proposal, it wanted to know how much it might cost the government or affect taxes.
"As the largest group of taxpayers to the Fund, ... API members cannot conclude their evaluation of the legislation without fully understanding these cost ramifications," it said.
The group said that if the government was going to have to pay for more cleanups, other reforms should be approved to cut overall programme costs, including making cleanups cheaper.

API supported the Republicans' proposal to eliminate rules that make permanent removal of hazardous waste at a site the preferred cleanup standard and to use cost estimates as one of the factors in setting cleanup plans for a site.
It also called for a strict $50 million cap on natural resource damages that companies could be forced to pay as a result of hazardous waste problems.
